newsitem.title: bangladesh: Bangladesh-rebel talks spur hopes of peace.
newsitem.headline: Bangladesh-rebel talks spur hopes of peace.

text.p: The Bangladesh government and Shanti Bahini tribal rebels fighting for self-rule in the Chittagong Hill Tracts are to hold their first meeting in Dhaka on Saturday, with hopes for a peaceful settlement running high.
"We are expecting good progress in the peace talks," one official, who declined to be identified, said on Friday.

"That the Shanti Bahini has agreed to send its leaders to Dhaka for a dialogue itself is an encouraging sign. The ice has started melting and we expect a quick end to the 23-year-old insurgency," he said.
Previous meetings between the two sides have taken place in the hill town of Khagrachhari.

The Shanti Bahini (Peace Force) has fought a bush war for autonomy in the 5,500 sq miles (14,200 sq km) of Hill Tracts, bordering India and Burma, since 1973. They also want 300,000 Bengali-speaking settlers expelled from the area.
Officials say more than 8,500 rebels, soldiers and civilians have been killed in the insurgency, which has forced some 50,000 tribespeople to seek refuge in the northeast Indian state of Tripura.

Jyotirindra Budhipriya Larma, head of the Shanti Bahini's political wing, will head the five or 10-member rebel team at the talks, while Abul Hasanat Abdullah, a senior official of the ruling Awami League, will lead the government side.

A.B.M. Mohiuddin Chowdhury, mayor of Chittagong and a member of the government team, said he hoped the talks would end fruitfully as Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina was ready to accept most of the insurgents' demands.
"However, the government will not surrender national interests for reaching any accord, especially when it comes to the army or lawful settlers," he told Reuters without elaborating.
Official sources said the government, at the request of the rebels, was keeping the meeting venue a secret.
"They (rebels) want their leaders heavily protected. We have to listen to their security propositions," one said.
The rebel team will fly to Dhaka by military helicopter from Dudukchhari, a Hill Tracts village near the Indian border.

They would fly back to Dudukchhari after the talks, one official said, without indicating how long the meeting may last. "It may be a one-day affair or spread over several days. It all depends on the progress of the talks," he said.
A Hill Tracts official said: "If the cherished peace accord is reached or at least visibly within sight, the rebel leaders are expected to meet Hasina and Home Minister Rafiqul Islam."
Sources close to the meeting said Bangladesh might accept the Shanti Bahini's demand for a gradual withdrawal of government troops from the Hill Tracts, but not the demand to expel settlers.

"We will try to convince (the rebels) that they would be given full social and cultural rights, but they must live together with Bengalis moved into the Hill Tracts under government plans," one source said.
"The rebels should also promise to stop using guns, scaring away tribespeople and trying to provoke anti-government sentiment," the source said.
